 Claim Social Security at 62 and the Check Is 70% of the Full Amount. Wait Until 70 and It’s 124%. Here’s the Table for a Retiree Whose Pension Covers the Basics
 Jake FitzGerald Fri, November 20, 2026 at 4:53 AM EST 5 min read Quick Read 
 A $60,000 pension pushes 85% of Social Security into taxable income at every claiming age, so delaying raises taxable benefits too. 
 Waiting until 70 pays off in total dollars only after about age 80 versus claiming at 62, and about 82 versus 67. 
 A widow inherits up to 100% of her late husband's check, so his claiming age sets her income: $3,472 versus $1,960.

 Social Security lets you start retirement benefits at 62. Delayed retirement credits stop growing at 70, so the choice of start month falls somewhere in that eight-year window and can't easily be changed once checks begin. If a FERS annuity already covers the fixed bills, three factors drive this decision: how long you live, what your spouse would receive as a survivor, and how Social Security adds to pension income for federal tax. 
 Michael Vi / iStock Editorial via Getty Images Full Retirement Age Is 67 for Anyone Born in 1960 or Later 
 For workers born in 1960 or later, SSA sets full retirement age at 67. SSA's reduction rules cut the check to 70% of the full amount at 62. Each month of delay past 67 adds a credit until the benefit reaches 124% at 70, and SSA says the monthly benefit stops increasing after that. 
 Assumptions: federal tax only (state tax changes), tax year 2025 rules, filing as a married couple, $60,000 FERS annuity, $2,800 monthly full benefit at 67, spouse's income kept out, no COLA, no growth.

 Pension Income Puts the Maximum 85% of Each Benefit on the Return 
 Story Continues IRS Publication 17 states that up to 85% of benefits become taxable once half the benefits plus all other income passes $44,000 for joint filers. In this example, a $60,000 annuity tops that line at every claiming age. Running the 2025 worksheet sets the taxable share at the 85% ceiling in every row, because the annuity alone meets the lower thresholds. 
 Even the age-70 row leaves room. After the 2025 joint standard deduction of $31,500, taxable income comes to $63,914.40. The 2025 joint 12% bracket runs to $96,950, which leaves $33,035.60 for TSP withdrawals or Roth conversions before the 22% rate applies. For 2027 Part B premiums, the income-related surcharge starts above $224,000 of joint modified adjusted gross income. Pension income and taxable Social Security both count toward that figure. 
 Delay Pulls Ahead on Cumulative Dollars After Age 80 
 With no COLA and no discounting, the age-70 claimant's total payments pass the age-62 total at age 80.37, and pass the age-67 total at 82.5. Claiming early fits people with shorter expected lifespans, single retirees with no survivor depending on the check, and couples where the spouse's own benefit is the larger one. Delay suits a higher earner who expects to live well into his 80s or has a younger spouse. 
 The 2026 Trustees Report projects that combined Social Security reserves run out in the third quarter of 2034. After that, 83% of scheduled benefits would be paid. Applied to the table, a $3,472 check would pay $2,881.76 and a $1,960 check would pay $1,626.80. 
 Survivor Check Carries the Claiming Age Forward 
 SSA says a surviving spouse can receive up to 100% of the deceased spouse's benefit at the survivor's own full retirement age. A widow at that age who inherits a $3,472 check keeps $3,472. If the claim was made at 62, she keeps $1,960. SSA also says survivor and retirement payments won't be added together, so she gets whichever is larger. 
 Each Choice Closes on a Fixed Date 
 Age 62: The earliest month you can claim. SSA requires you to be 62 for the entire month. 
 Age 65: Anyone delaying Social Security still needs to apply for Medicare within 3 months of the 65th birthday, or Part B and Part D can cost more. 
 Age 70: Delayed retirement credits stop. 
 Age 75: Required distributions from the TSP begin for those born in 1960 or later, under 26 U.S.C. § 401(a)(9)(C)(v)(II). 
 The earliest of these deadlines is the month you turn 62 for the whole month. Any retirement application filed with SSA after that point sets the reduction percentage, and SSA's chart then applies that percentage to every check that follows.
